title: Eighty Crowns on the Ninepins
blurb: Dagny Quillon has never held a Pin in a match, but her brother has borrowed eighty crowns against a team that just lost its Anchor.

blocks.text: Wat Ellery walked out of Shaft Nine an hour before the bell, and his new boots squeaked all the way across the yard.
Hal said his name once. Wat didn't turn round. He went out through the gate, and the squeak went with him.
Beside me, my brother went very still. Rafe is never still.
"Dags," he said. "I've got eighty crowns on the Ninepins. Borrowed."
I felt it in my throat first. It shut, the way it shuts when you swallow something too big. Then the cold came into my hands. Then I did the sum, because the sum is what I do when I'm frightened.

Eighty crowns, borrowed from Sibbald Teague this week. Four crowns a week on top. All of it due on the day of the Step, eight weeks off: a hundred and twelve crowns. The Ninepins had one Anchor left now, Hal Stenning, and the Gallowsgate Coopers had two. One Anchor against two loses. Everybody in that yard knew it. If the Ninepins lost, Rafe's money was gone and the debt stayed, and it would grow every week until the day Teague came to collect it, and Teague would be polite about it, and that was the part that made my knees go soft.

There was a worse part, and I couldn't say it to him. The odds Rafe had bet on were mine. Three weeks before, I'd worked out the Ninepins' chances on the back of a coal chit at our kitchen table, every side's wins and losses from last season, and I'd left the chit where he would see it. I knew he'd read it. I knew what he would do with it. I left it there anyway. He doesn't know that.
"I'm able," I said.
Rafe stared at me. "You've never held a Pin in a match. Not once. And your hand, Dags. You can't climb, can you?"
"Lisbet can rope me."
He didn't argue. That frightened me more than anything he could have said.
Sibbald Teague was standing on the Lip when we came down the ladder, beside the Weighman's platform, in a good grey coat. He is a soft-spoken man. He bowed his head to me as if I were somebody.

"Abel Quillon's girl," he said. "Dagny Quillon. Plumbed on the second Tuesday after the thaw, four years ago, in the long room over the Weighhouse stables. Able. Never signed." He smiled. "Your father saw to that. Your father always knew what a cage weighed."

It landed in my hands like cold water. My father ran the Settle lift until its cable parted, two years ago. I wear his lift-coat. I didn't know why a man who lends money would want to talk about my father's cage, and I didn't like that he knew which room I'd stood in at fourteen.

Teague turned to my brother. "Rafe Quillon. Eighty crowns. Eighty-four a week from today. A hundred and twelve on the day of the Step." He said it gently, like a man reading out a hymn number. "It would be a shame."
Then he walked away along the Lip to watch with his Tallymen, and I could breathe again.
Hal Stenning was by the ladder, coughing. He coughed with one hand pressed flat to his side, and when he saw me looking he took the hand away.
"A liability," he said to Gaffer Osk, not to me. "Never trained. Can't climb. Can't—" He coughed again. "Can't throw."

"Liability, is it?" said Dunnet Haig, and laughed, big and loud, so the Coopers on the far side of the Lip looked over. "But I heard her at the gate, counting under her breath like a tally clerk. Counts, that's you now. Welcome to Shaft Nine, Counts."

Dunnet and Lisbet went up and winched Gaffer Osk's chair down from the yard, beside the ladder. It's a small chair. It took the two of them and the winch, and the winch rope groaned. Everybody in Scarrow knows it's packed with lead. When they set it on the Lip planks, the grit on the boards crept in to its legs and lay round each one in a little ring. I saw it. I didn't know what I was seeing.
Osk looked up at me from the chair. His voice was low and slow, and the Lip went quiet to hear it.
"One," he said. "Whole hand on the Pin. Two. Watch their Anchor. Not the Cob. The Anchor." He waited a long time. "Three. Never hold more than you can... carry."
That was all. Three steps and no more. Nobody said anything about letting go.

The Weighman put me on the Lip scale. "Eight stone six," he said, and wrote it in the league book, and wrote a word beside my name. "Emergency clause. Result stands if she's registered inside seven days."
Lisbet Garrow put me in a sling, quick and rough. "Hands in. Don't grab the rope with the bad one. Move."

She lowered me to L5, a ledge three metres deep with a chalk circle round the Pin and a lamp hung on the wall. Above me the shaft went up into the dark. Below me, across the shaft, was the Coopers' L6, and under that the Throat and the two wells.

I put my right hand on the Pin, the whole of it, the way Osk said. My left hand stayed in my coat pocket. Its ring and little fingers don't close; they haven't since a cage gate crushed them when I was twelve. The Pin was cold, and then it wasn't, and I felt the whole zone come into my hand, every metre of air from the floor of my ledge to the ledge above, the way you feel a full bucket you've lifted.
The bell went.

I was slow in Drop 1. I was slow and I knew it, and knowing it didn't help. The Coopers' Anchor, Brannock, held L4 across the shaft from me, and every time he turned, I turned after him, and after is too late. He pinned Dunnet flat on our wall for sixty counts and the Weighman called the point. Then the Cob came down past my ledge into our side of the Throat, and I heard it go into our well like a door slamming.
Four nil.
Lisbet hauled me up for the Hoist. My knees ached a little and my wrist ached a lot. The Weighman read the scale: nine stone and a pound. Nine pounds of carry, in one Drop, for nothing.
Rafe was at the rail. He didn't say anything. His face was white.
Walls swapped for Drop 2. I took L6, the lowest ledge on our side, above our own well. Brannock took L5 across from me, and our two zones met in the Lap between us.
This time I watched him, the way Osk said. Not the Cob. The Anchor.

Their Caller was a big-voiced woman in a cooper's apron. She shouted every turn. And Brannock always turned one count after she shouted. Always. Call, one, hands. I counted it four times to be sure, under my breath, the way I count when I'm frightened.

So I stopped watching his hands and listened to her voice instead. When she called, I turned. A set turns a quarter-turn every three counts, so one count is thirty degrees, and thirty degrees in a Lap is the difference between a man swinging into a wall and a man swinging past it.
"Evens on the left!" Pru called down from the Lip. "Seven-to-two he's late! Dunnet, long!"

The counting didn't make me less afraid. I want to be honest about that. My heart was going so hard I could feel it in the Pin. What the counting did was keep the fear out of my hands, so my hands could do the work.
Dunnet swung across on his rope with the Cob under his arm. Brannock was a count late. Thirty degrees. Dunnet let go over their side of the Throat and the Cob went into their well.
Four, three.
At the Hoist I weighed nine stone eight. A stone and two pounds of carry since the bell. I could feel every pound of it in the backs of my legs.
Pru read the Coopers' numbers off the Weighman's board. "Brannock's carrying six stone twelve. Evens he's sore. Long odds he's happy."
"Coopers," said Dunnet, and grinned at their bench. "I bet their barrels leak too."
We were behind, so we chose our wall for Drop 3. I asked for L5 again. I knew its stone now.
I didn't tell anybody my plan. I should have. I didn't, because Osk would have said three, and I already knew what three was.

I'd watched the Coopers' Dropper, Tull, all through Drops 1 and 2. A wiry man, eleven stone at most. At the bell he always went down early on his own wall, fast, to get under the Cob. Always. If Tull was flat on a wall, the Coopers had no Dropper. Then the only thing between the Cob and their well was Brannock's set. And every head Brannock turned would cost him a stone a minute, and he was carrying near seven already.
It would cost me a stone a minute too. Tull was one head. One head, one plumb, one stone every minute I held him.
The bell went.

I turned the moment it rang. Three counts for the quarter-turn, and my zone's down lay over sideways toward the far wall, a little round from their rope line, so the low place on that curved stone was three metres from any rope.
Tull came down into my zone and fell sideways onto the far wall. A short fall. He was a metre off it. He hit and lay there flat, as if the wall were a floor, and the Weighman began to count.

He crawled for the rope. I tipped my set a few degrees and he slid back down the curve. Never enough to lift him off the stone. If I lifted him off the stone, he'd be in free fall, and turning on a man in free fall is a foul. So I tipped and he slid, and I tipped and he slid.
Sixty counts. The Weighman called the point. Four, four.
I didn't let go. If I let go, Tull was back in play.

I felt the first stone arrive in my knees. It didn't hurt. It was weight, that's all, as if someone had hung a full coal sack from each knee by a hook. Then the second stone came, and that one hurt, a hot ache behind both kneecaps, and I said it out loud so I'd know it was real.
"Two stone. One head. Two minutes."

Up above, the Coopers' other Anchor was holding the Cob high, up by L2, and Hal was fighting him for it from L3. I could hear Hal humming his one low note. I knew what the Coopers wanted. At the five-minute bell, if the Cob was still above the floor of L4, the Weighman would call the Letgo, and every Pin would be let go for ten counts. Mine too. Tull would go free. Everything I'd paid would be for nothing.
"Three stone. Three minutes."
The third stone went into my hips. I couldn't feel the cold in my hands any more. I could feel the cold in the lining of my father's coat, against my back, where the sweat had soaked through.
"Four minutes. Four stone."

That was the worst one. My knees bent on their own. I went down onto them inside the chalk circle, because if I left the mark while gripping the Pin they'd give the Coopers a point, and I would not give them a point. My right hand stayed on the Pin. I was more frightened than I have ever been, and I could say exactly of what: of my knees, of the bones in my feet, of Rafe's face at the rail if I failed.
"Cage loaded, Da," I said. "Hold the brake."
He used to say that into the speaking tube at the top of the Settle lift, every run. Nobody answered me.
"Low!" Pru screamed from the Lip. "Dunnet, low, it's yours, go, go!"

Hal had knocked the Cob loose. Dunnet caught it in L3 and came down the far wall rope with it, through my zone, past Tull, walking down the stone on his rope as if it were a road, because in my zone it was. Eleven counts. Dunnet is a head and a half and the Cob is half a head, and I paid for every count. I felt it go into my shins.

Then he was below me, past the Lap, sliding down the rope past the L6 ledge on their wall and in under it. Brannock turned his zone over to straight up, six counts for the half-turn, and he started a count late as always. Dunnet fell upward into the underside of the L6 ledge and stuck there with the Cob hugged to his belly and one hand on the rope, so they couldn't count him for a pin. A metre above the Throat. A metre from their well.
The five-minute bell rang. The Cob was under L4. No Letgo. I didn't have to let go. Part of me had wanted the Letgo, so that the choice would be taken out of my hand, and I am ashamed of that.
Brannock was holding two heads straight up. Two stone a minute, on top of near seven. I did his sum as well as mine. I couldn't help it. I knew now what a stone felt like coming in.
Their Caller knew it too. I heard her breathing between calls. She lasted twenty counts. Then thirty.
"Brannock," she said, not loud. "Let it go."
One count. Then his hand opened. His zone went true. Dunnet dropped a metre on his rope, opened his arms, and the Cob fell into the Coopers' well.
Seven, four.
I opened my hand.
Nobody had taught me the Release. I didn't know there was anything to teach. I just opened my hand the ordinary way, and the zone went out of it, and I was a girl kneeling on a ledge in the dark.
Five stone and two pounds in that one hold. Six stone and four, near enough, since the first bell. I counted it under my breath twice, and it came out the same both times.
Rafe came down the rope from the Lip like he'd been born on one. He was whooping before his feet touched the ledge.

"Did you see Brannock's face, Dags? Like a man watching his own coffin go down the shaft, wasn't it? And their Caller, did you see her? I've never seen a woman look so much like a dropped pie, have you?"

I tried to stand and couldn't. My knees wouldn't take it. I sat on the stone with my back against the wall and counted under my breath, because I was frightened, and the counting was the only thing holding my hands still.
Rafe stopped. "Dags. You're all right, aren't you?"
"About six stone of carry," I said. "I can't climb."
I didn't say anything after it. I didn't have anything to put after it.
His face changed. Then Lisbet's voice came down from above. "She's too heavy to haul by hand. I'll get the harness and the winch. Rafe, up, you're in my way. Move."
"Go on," I said to him. "Go and get your money."

He went, because he's sixteen, and he'd won, and he couldn't stop grinning. I watched him climb, fast and easy, and I loved his stupid, happy face so much my chest hurt, and I was frightened for him, because a face like that is how you end up owing Sibbald Teague eighty crowns in the first place.
Then I was alone on L5. The lamp hissed. Up on the Lip they were cheering, very far away.
Something moved by my boot.

Grit. The loose grit on the ledge was sliding across the stone toward me, slowly, in little lines. Chalk dust from the mark drifted in after it. A penny had fallen from my father's coat pocket when I went down on my knees. It slid back across the stone, all by itself, and stopped against my boot.
Nobody in Shaft Nine was holding a Pin, and down was pointing at me.
